content: 1. If feasible, discard urine and record the output on a whiteboard as per Appendix F. If quantifying urine output is not possible, document the frequency of urination. 2. For severe confirmed or suspected cases of Ebola with emergency signs (including Lassa fever, Marburg, or Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever), manage patients with intensive supportive care. Document clinical data daily on a patient monitoring form. 3. Recognize general signs of shock in viral hemorrhagic fever (VHF) patients, such as a fast, weak pulse; pallor or cold extremities; prolonged capillary refill time (>3 seconds); dizziness or inability to stand; decreased urine output (<30 mL/hour); difficulty breathing; impaired consciousness (lethargy, agitation, confusion); and low systolic blood pressure (SBP <90 mmHg). Assess these signs in the context of the patient’s pre-morbid state, pregnancy, age, and medication history. 4. Pregnant women, patients with chronic illnesses, or others with a baseline SBP <90 mmHg but normal mental status, capillary refill, and urine output do not necessarily have shock. Seek assistance from the most experienced clinician available if an Ebola patient develops shock. 5. VHF patients may experience shock due to hypovolemia from gastrointestinal (GI) losses (common in the 2014–2015 West African Ebola outbreak), septic shock, hemorrhagic shock (less common), or a combination of these. The pathophysiology and management of septic shock in VHF are similar to those caused by bacterial infections. 6. Intensive supportive care, including fluid resuscitation and electrolyte replacement, is critical for managing hypovolemia from large GI losses. Most Ebola patients develop vomiting and diarrhea, with some experiencing severe GI illness leading to rapid dehydration, hypokalemia, and acidosis. If untreated, these abnormalities can result in death from hypovolemic shock and metabolic derangements. 7. Assess dehydration by checking for lethargy, poor or eager drinking, sunken eyes, and slow skin pinch recoil (>2 seconds). Examine stool or vomit containers for large-volume GI losses. 8. Classify dehydration severity in Ebola patients: Severe dehydration: Two or more signs such as lethargy, sunken eyes, inability to drink, or very slow skin pinch recoil. Treat with IV fluid resuscitation and oral rehydration salts (ORS). Some dehydration: Signs like sunken eyes, thirst, slow skin pinch recoil, or restlessness in children. Start IV fluids and continue ORS and feeding. No dehydration: Provide ORS and food. 9. For large GI losses, administer IV fluids aggressively to match losses. Do not wait for dehydration signs before starting or increasing IV fluids. Use Lactated Ringer’s solution (Hartmann’s solution) as the fluid of choice. Place an 18G or larger IV catheter in the largest available peripheral vein, avoiding the antecubital fossa if possible. 10. For adults, give a 1-liter IV fluid bolus over 30 minutes or faster. Reassess for dehydration and shock signs after the bolus. Repeat crystalloid boluses if shock persists. Severely ill adults with large GI losses may require 3–6 liters of fluid daily. Monitor for fluid overload and adjust hydration targets accordingly. 11. Monitor hydration targets in adults, including heart rate (<100 bpm), urine output (>30 mL/hour), SBP (>90 mmHg), capillary refill (<3 seconds), absence of skin mottling, palpable peripheral pulses, warm extremities, and improved mental status. Check IV infusion needs every 8 hours and reduce to maintenance levels when shock resolves. 12. Address electrolyte and glucose abnormalities. Hypokalemia from GI losses can cause arrhythmias, cardiac arrest, or seizures. Use point-of-care testing for electrolytes where possible. Add potassium chloride (KCl) to IV fluids empirically if hypokalemia is suspected. Provide oral potassium supplements (40 mEq/day) for patients tolerating oral intake. Correct hypomagnesemia to assist with hypokalemia correction. 13. Monitor for hypoglycemia, especially in critically ill adults, children, elderly, or malnourished patients. Check glucose levels with a bedside glucometer and replenish as needed. Empirically administer glucose if lethargy, seizures, or coma develop. 14. Consider empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) for patients with significant abdominal symptoms or suspected sepsis. Add metronidazole for worsening GI complaints or bloody diarrhea in non-confirmed Ebola cases. Discontinue antibiotics after 5 days if symptoms improve and no other indications exist. 15. Managing septic shock in Ebola patients is challenging due to overlapping etiologies like hypovolemia and secondary infections. Clinical diagnosis of septic shock includes suspected infection, hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg), and signs like tachycardia (>100 bpm), tachypnea (>24 breaths/min), or abnormal temperature (<36°C or >38°C). 16. Provide oxygen therapy if available, titrating to SpO2 ≥90%. Administer rapid IV fluids (e.g., Lactated Ringer’s or Normal Saline) at 20 mL/kg/hour, up to 60 mL/kg within the first 2 hours. If SBP remains <90 mmHg after fluids, consider vasopressors if feasible and continue fluids at 5–10 mL/kg/hour. 17. Treat infections urgently with empirical antimicrobials, including antibiotics, antimalarials (if malaria is suspected or confirmed), and antivirals (e.g., ribavirin for confirmed Lassa fever or CCHF). Identify and treat additional infection sources using clinical signs, chest X-rays, or other diagnostic tools if available. 18. Monitor patients every 30 minutes until stable, then hourly. Record SBP, pulse, respiratory rate, SpO2, mental status, jugular venous pressure, and auscultation findings. Address laboratory abnormalities like hemoglobin <7 mg/dL or glucose <3 mmol/L promptly.
